intro: To format cells as currency in Numbers on Mac, select the cells, click Format in the toolbar, click the Cell tab, then pick Currency from the Data Format pop-up menu. Then set Decimals, the negative-value style and the currency symbol so the numbers read the way you want.
tldr: Select the cells, click Format in the toolbar, then open the Cell tab.
Click the Data Format pop-up menu and choose Currency. Cells show two decimal places by default.
Set Decimals, the negative-value style, the separator and the Currency symbol.
Numbers rounds the display only. Calculations still use the full value.
There is no keyboard shortcut for the currency format itself, so you work in the sidebar with the mouse or trackpad.

blocks.text: A currency format changes how a number looks, not what it is. A cell that shows $1,419.00 still holds the value you typed, so formulas and totals keep working. You can format a whole column of prices at once and still add it up. The steps in this guide use the Mac app. Numbers for iCloud in a browser uses slightly different labels, and those get their own section below.
Where the currency controls live on Mac

Numbers keeps cell formats in the Format sidebar. Click Format in the toolbar to open it. If the sidebar is hidden, choose View > Inspector > Show Inspector. Apple's sidebar help uses the same menu path to hide and show it. Once the sidebar is open, the Cell tab holds the Data Format pop-up menu you need.

Keep the cells selected while you change the format. The sidebar applies its settings to the selection, so check the selection before you pick Currency. A format applied to the wrong cells is easy to miss in a large sheet.
What each currency option does
Once you choose Currency, five controls appear. Each one changes how the number looks. None of them changes the value stored in the cell.

items: Decimals: sets how many decimal places show. The default is two. Click the down arrow until it reaches Auto to show as many decimals as you typed.
Negative value pop-up, to the right of Decimals: chooses how negative numbers look.
Thousands Separator: adds commas to large numbers, such as 1,419.
Accounting Style: shows negative values in parentheses instead of with a minus sign.
Currency pop-up menu: chooses the symbol, for example US Dollar ($).

blocks.text: Turn options on one at a time. Check the cell after each change before you add the next. That makes it clear which setting caused a surprise.
Decimals and rounding: what you see is not the full value

Numbers rounds the displayed value. It does not cut off the extra digits. If you set zero decimals, 5.75 shows as 6. The underlying value stays 5.75, and calculations use that number. This is why a total can look one unit off from the visible numbers.

blocks.caption: Examples from Apple's rounding rule and the Auto setting.

blocks.text: A column of rounded prices can add up to a total you do not expect. Check the sum against the typed values before you send the sheet. Auto is the safer choice while you build a sheet. Set a fixed number of decimals once the data is final.
Negative numbers and Accounting Style

Negative numbers need their own setting. The pop-up menu to the right of Decimals controls how they appear. Accounting Style goes further. It shows negative values in parentheses instead of with a minus sign. Pick one style for the whole table so readers do not have to guess.
Use the same negative style in every table in a workbook. A mix of minus signs and parentheses looks like an error, even when the numbers are correct.
Custom currency formats for unusual symbols

The built-in list does not cover every case. For a symbol or rule that Numbers does not list, make a custom format. Click the Data Format pop-up menu and choose Create Custom Format. Name the format, pick a Type, then click OK. The Type choices are Number, Date & Time, or Text.

Number formats can hold up to three rules. Three rules can cover positive, negative and zero values with different looks. To change a format later, open the same pop-up menu and choose Edit Custom Format. If you choose Delete Format, cells that used it revert to automatic, so check those cells afterward.
Numbers for iCloud: the same format under the Data tab

Numbers for iCloud is the browser version. Its guide puts the controls in a different place. Select a cell or range, then click Data at the top of the Format sidebar. Click the Data Format pop-up menu and choose Currency. The rest matches the Mac app: Decimals, the negative value option, Accounting Style or Thousands Separator, and the Currency pop-up menu.

Apple's iCloud guide does not name a version, and it lists no keyboard shortcuts for this task. If the labels on your screen differ from either guide, match the words, not the positions. Look for Data Format in whichever tab holds it.
Common problems with currency cells in Numbers

The most common report is a currency cell that shows far too many digits. One Apple Community user on Numbers 11.2 typed 14.19 and saw $1419.00. Replies blamed mismatched decimal and currency separator settings. The original poster said matching those settings in System Settings fixed it. The thread has no formal accepted answer.

A second report is a cell that keeps going back to text. In a thread about Numbers 3.5.3, replies linked the problem to a region that uses commas as decimal marks. One user said switching the decimal separator to a comma fixed it. The suggested fix was to check Language & Region and then restart. That thread has no accepted answer either.
Both threads are old user reports, not official fixes. Use them as clues. Both point at region and number settings, so start there.
Keyboard shortcuts, and why there is none for currency

Apple's Numbers shortcut list has no key combination for the currency format. You will use the Format sidebar with the mouse or trackpad. Shortcuts help with the sidebar itself. Control-Grave (`) moves to the next sidebar tab, and Shift-Control-Grave moves back to the previous one.

The shortcut list also gives Option-Command-I for hiding or showing the sidebar. Apple's sidebar help gives only the View menu path and no shortcut. Those two pages disagree, so test Option-Command-I on your Mac before you rely on it.
Mistakes people make with currency cells

items: Expecting a text cell to change. A cell that stays text needs a region check, not another format click.
Trusting the display. A rounded cell still holds the full value, so check the typed number when a total looks wrong.
Mixing negative styles. Use one style across the workbook so readers see a consistent pattern.
Deleting a custom format without checking its cells. Deleted formats send their cells back to automatic.
Ignoring region settings. Decimal and currency separators come from System Settings, so a sheet can look different on a Mac with other settings.

blocks.text: Check your Numbers version before you follow a guide

Apple's Mac guide was written for Numbers 15.4, and Apple's Mac guide welcome page states that same version. The Mac App Store lists Numbers 15.4.2, released Oct 23, and it needs macOS 26.0 or later. The currency menu labels were not confirmed for 15.4.2 specifically, so compare what you see with these steps.
If a label differs, look for the same word in the Format sidebar. The menu names in the steps are the ones Apple uses, so a close match is usually the right control.
Use currency cells in formulas and when you share

Currency formatting is a display setting. You can build totals, averages and other formulas on the same cells. For a walkthrough, read [how to add a formula to a cell in Numbers on Mac](/how-to/add-a-formula-to-a-cell-in-numbers).

If the sheet goes to someone else, check how it looks before you send it. When you need a fixed copy, read the steps for [exporting a spreadsheet to PDF in Numbers](/how-to/export-a-spreadsheet-to-pdf-in-numbers) first.
Where to go next

Start with one column. Format it, type a test value, and check the display. Once it looks right, format the rest of the sheet the same way. To flag negative or large values in color, read [how to highlight cells in Numbers on Mac with conditional rules](/how-to/highlight-cells-with-conditional-rules-in-numbers).

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to format cells as currency in Numbers on Mac?
faq.answer: No. Apple's keyboard shortcut list has no key combination for the currency format. Use the Format sidebar, the Cell tab and the Data Format pop-up menu instead. Shortcuts only help with the sidebar itself, such as moving between its tabs.

faq.question: Does formatting cells as currency change the number in the cell?
faq.answer: No. Numbers rounds the display, not the stored value. A cell set to zero decimals can show 6 while the value stays 5.75, and calculations use 5.75.

faq.question: Why does my currency cell show two decimal places?
faq.answer: Two is the default for currency cells in Numbers on Mac. To show as many decimals as you typed in each cell, click the Decimals down arrow until it reaches Auto. You can also delete the number in the Decimals field.

faq.question: Why does 14.19 show as $1419.00 in my currency cell?
faq.answer: A user on Numbers 11.2 reported this in an Apple Community thread. Replies blamed mismatched decimal and currency separator settings. Match those settings in System Settings, then check the cell again.

faq.question: Where is the currency option in Numbers for iCloud?
faq.answer: Click Data at the top of the Format sidebar, then open the Data Format pop-up menu and choose Currency. The Mac app puts the same menu under the Cell tab.

faq.question: Can I make my own currency format in Numbers on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Select the cells, go to the Cell tab, click the Data Format pop-up menu and choose Create Custom Format. Number formats can have up to three rules.

faq.question: Which Numbers version do these steps match?
faq.answer: Apple's Mac guide was written for Numbers 15.4. The Mac App Store lists Numbers 15.4.2, which needs macOS 26.0 or later. Compare the labels on your screen with these steps.

task: Format cells as currency in Numbers on Mac
appliesTo: Numbers for Mac: Apple's guide is written for 15.4, and the App Store lists 15.4.2 (macOS 26.0 or later)
requirements: A Mac running macOS 26.0 or later for the current Numbers app
Numbers installed from the Mac App Store
At least one cell with a number in it

steps.name: Select the cells
steps.text: Click the first cell in the range, then drag across the cells you want to format. Keep the selection active while you change the format.
steps.tip: Format before you fill in the numbers if you can, so you can check the display as you type.

steps.name: Open the Format sidebar
steps.text: Click Format in the toolbar. If the sidebar is hidden, choose View > Inspector > Show Inspector.
steps.tip: Use View > Inspector > Hide Inspector to close the sidebar when you want more room.

steps.name: Click the Cell tab
steps.text: At the top of the Format sidebar, click the Cell tab. In the Mac app, the currency options live here, not under Data.
steps.tip: Numbers for iCloud uses the Data tab for the same options.

steps.name: Open the Data Format pop-up menu
steps.text: Under the Cell tab, click the Data Format pop-up menu. This menu lists the formats that Numbers offers for the selected cells.

steps.name: Choose Currency
steps.text: Choose Currency from the Data Format list. The selected cells switch to currency format with two decimal places by default.

steps.name: Set the decimal places
steps.text: Find Decimals in the sidebar. Leave it at two, or click the down arrow until it reaches Auto to show as many decimals as you typed in each cell.
steps.tip: Auto is useful while you test values. A fixed number is easier to read in a finished table.

steps.name: Choose how negatives look
steps.text: Open the pop-up menu to the right of Decimals and pick the style for negative values. Then select the Accounting Style checkbox if you want parentheses.
steps.tip: Use one negative style across the whole workbook.

steps.name: Turn on Thousands Separator
steps.text: Select the Thousands Separator checkbox if you want commas in large numbers, such as 1,419.

steps.name: Pick the currency symbol
steps.text: Click the Currency pop-up menu and choose your symbol, such as US Dollar ($).

steps.name: Type a test value
steps.text: Type 14.19 into one formatted cell and check that it displays as 14.19 with your symbol. If it shows a much larger number, check the separator settings in System Settings.
steps.tip: A number that shows 100 times too large is a separator mismatch, not a formatting bug.

steps.name: Create a custom format if you need one
steps.text: For a symbol or rule the list does not cover, click Data Format and choose Create Custom Format. Name it, pick a Type, then click OK.
steps.tip: Number formats can have up to three rules.

troubleshooting.fix: Open System Settings and check Language & Region. Make sure the decimal and currency separators match the numbers you type. An Apple Community user on Numbers 11.2 fixed it this way, but the thread has no formal accepted answer.

troubleshooting.problem: A cell stays text and will not become currency
troubleshooting.fix: Check Language & Region for a region that uses commas as decimal marks. One user on Numbers 3.5.3 said switching the decimal separator to a comma fixed it, and the suggested fix includes a restart. These are user reports, not official fixes.

troubleshooting.problem: The menu names in a guide do not match your screen
troubleshooting.fix: Compare your version with the guide. Apple's Mac guide was written for 15.4, and the App Store lists 15.4.2. Look for the same option name in the Format sidebar.

troubleshooting.problem: A total looks off by a unit or a cent
troubleshooting.fix: Check the display rounding. Set Decimals to Auto to see the typed values. Calculations use the full value, not the rounded display.
Apple's sidebar help gives only View > Inspector and lists no shortcut for it. Use View > Inspector > Show Inspector, or click Format in the toolbar.
